steps: Permits & site rules
Install to CAN/CSA-B365 and local code, with local building officials' approval first. Never in a fireplace, and never connected to an air distribution duct or system.
Unpack & check
Confirm the fire bricks haven't shifted, the air control works freely and the baffles are placed correctly. The glove and ceramic flue connection gasket ship in the ashpan or firebox.
Chimney
Dedicated flue: listed HT (UL-103) or code-approved masonry with liner, not less than 6" inside, independently secured. At least 16 feet above the stove is recommended.
Choose top or rear outlet
For rear: knock out the round panel in the rear heat shield plate, swap the blanking plate and flue collar, then push down and tighten the enclosed screws.
Chimney connector
6 inches (150mm), 24 gauge or heavier single wall (never galvanized) or listed double wall; three screws per joint, rise 1/4 inch per foot, no more than two 90 degree turns, 8 feet total.
Position for clearances
Set the stove to the clearance table for your connector and layout; keep furniture 30 inches away.

Pick the table for your connector and layout:

  • Standard residential, single- or double-wall connector (p. 8)
  • Rear vent out back wall, single-wall connector (p. 9)
  • Alcove, double-wall connector only, max depth 32" (p. 9)

Keep furniture at least 30 inches away (p. 9). Near non-combustible walls, a gap of 4 inches or more is recommended.
Floor protection
Non-combustible ember protection beneath the stove, 16" to the front and 6" to the sides (US). With a rear exit, also beneath the connector and 2 inches beyond each side.
Mobile home (US only)
Outside combustion air kit, listed Type HT connector and chimney, spark-arrestor cap; bolt through the hearth pad into the flooring per 24 CFR, Part 3280.
Fresh-air inlet
Where room air leakage isn't enough, add a dedicated inlet with 2 square inches (1250 square mm) of free air space, away from negative-pressure walls and not directly across from the stove.
First fire
Keep it small so the paint cures and the plates settle; ventilate the room. Keep the fuel load below the secondary air supply box.

panels.title: Smoke or poor draft
items: Smoke or fumes when lighting or reloading → poor draft almost certainly to blame
Fire won't respond → poor draft; in a very few cases, too little fresh air into the room
Stove suddenly sluggish → soot fall around the flue collar or in the flue/chimney
Flue section significantly larger than 6" → flue gases cool; sluggish, unpredictable performance
Overly dry, gray wood → back-puffing and sluggishness

panels.title: Over-firing
items: Any part of the stove or chimney connector glows → over-firing
Flue temperature above 450° C (750°F) → over-firing, premature wear
Baffle distorted by an overfire → still works, efficiency compromised; replace it
Persistent heavy firing, or soot and ash left to build up → fast internal wear

panels.title: Dirty glass
items: Fuel too wet, or wood not well seasoned
Logs too large or not split
Combustion temperatures too low, or stove run too slowly
Wood spits or sizzles and the glass mists up → not properly seasoned

panels.title: Fire hard to control
items: Door gasket hardened, air leaking in around the door → replace with a Morsø rope gasket kit
Door difficult to close → replace the door gasket

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
A cold stove needs plenty of air to get going. Morsø recommends the top-down method: it's the most environmentally friendly way to light, and it keeps soot on the glass to a minimum.

  1. Lay about 2-4 lbs of dry kindling sticks. Put two firelighters directly under the top layer of kindling.
  2. Open the air supply fully: move the air control handle above the door all the way to the right.
  3. Light the fire.
  4. Partly close the door, leaving it open an inch or two so plenty of air gets in. Don't leave the stove while the door is open.
  5. After about 5-10 minutes, when the chimney is warm, close the door. A good layer of embers forms after about 15-20 minutes.

Your very first fire

Make sure the baffles are in place, then keep the first fire small. That lets the paint cure and the main plates of the stove settle into position. The paint gives off some fumes, so ventilate the room.

Note: p. 12 says to operate the stove only with the door fully closed, because of the risk of smoke and flame spillage; the lighting steps on pp. 14–15 say to leave the door open an inch or two while lighting.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
The handle above the door sets the primary air. It feeds preheated air into the firebox through the airwash system above the glass.

All the way rightfully open: for lighting and reloading
Mid rangemedium burn rate
All the way leftclosed: the minimum low burn rate

The secondary air is fixed open and can't be adjusted. It's injected above the fire for cleaner, more efficient burning.

Turning it down

A few minutes after a fresh load catches, set the air for the heat you want. Always leave enough air for clear, enduring flames. Before you go all the way to the minimum, burn at medium for about 15 minutes so the fire is properly established.

Rule of thumb: less heat, less wood, less air. More heat, more wood, more air. Keep a good layer of embers either way.

Don't modify it. The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory, and altering it is against federal regulations. Never try to get more heat by altering the air control's adjustment range.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Add wood while there are still plenty of live embers. With a good layer of embers, the new wood should light within 2 minutes.

  1. Use a poker to spread the embers across the firebox floor, bringing plenty toward the front.
  2. Lay two pieces of wood on the embers, with half an inch or more between them.
  3. Close the door and leave the air control fully open. If the wood doesn't catch, leave the door slightly ajar until it does, then close it.
  4. After a few minutes, set the air control for the heat you want.

How much wood

The manual recommends loads of 3 lbs (2 pieces) up to 6 lbs (5 pieces). The maximum per load is 6 lbs (5 split logs).

Keep the load low. Always keep the wood below the stainless-steel air box on the back wall of the firebox. The space in front of and above it is reserved for burning the wood gases.
Note: pp. 15–16 give the load size as up to 6 lbs (5 pieces); p. 28 says to refuel with 2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg.

Don't leave the stove burning overnight. At low temperature the wood gases don't ignite; they settle as soot in the chimney and stove.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn only natural wood that is well seasoned and dry, with no more than 20% moisture. The Morsø Moisture Meter (part # 62929900) checks it.

Lengthmax 12 inches (30 cm)
Maker's website: Log Size 11".
Thicknessapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)

Once it's cut to length, split it down the middle so the moisture can escape.

Seasoning

Stack it under cover in an airy spot where air moves through each piece. Some soft woods season in one good summer; oak, maple and elm can take up to 18 months. Seasoned wood feels light and cracks from the center out at the ends. If it spits or sizzles and the glass keeps misting up, it isn't seasoned. Avoid overly dry, gray wood: it can cause back-puffing and sluggish burning.

Never burn

Garbage, lawn clippings or yard waste, anything with rubber (tires included), plastic or asbestos, waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners or asphalt products, pressure-treated wood or railroad ties, construction or demolition debris, salt-water driftwood or anything else previously saturated with salt water, manure or animal remains, unseasoned wood, paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard. Burning these may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Firelighters made of paper, sawdust or wax are fine for starting a fire.

Note: p. 12 gives the log thickness as approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm); p. 28 says the wood must be split and 8 - 12 cm thick.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Run the stove at the right temperatures and there should be little or no dirt on the glass. Dirt from lighting mostly burns off as the stove heats up.

For heavier deposits that won't burn off, use Morsø glass cleaner on cold glass, following its instructions. Never use abrasive cleaners.

Why glass gets dirty

  • The wood is too wet or not well seasoned.
  • The logs are too large or not split.
  • The fire burns too cool, or the stove is run too slowly.
Damaged glass: don't use the stove. Replace broken glass right away with the high-temperature ceramic glass Morsø supplies through your dealer.

Never clean the glass while it's hot. Avoid striking the glass or slamming the door. Old ceramic glass can't go in ordinary glass recycling: hand it in to a recycling station as ceramic glass.

ash.title: Emptying the ash pan
ash.html:
Empty the ash pan daily or as needed. Ash that builds up toward the underside of the grate traps heat and can make the grate fail early.

  1. Open the front door. Use a shovel or poker to stir excess ash through the ash slots in the grate into the ash pan.
  2. Take out the ash pan, keeping it level so ash doesn't spill.
  3. Empty it into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  4. Put the ash pan back and close the door.

Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all cinders have thoroughly cooled.

When you can, leave a 1-1.5 inch layer of ash on the firebox floor. It insulates the fire.
Never empty the stove while it's in operation, and never use a household or shop vacuum to remove ash.

chimney.title: Chimney care & creosote
chimney.html:
When wood burns slowly, it gives off tar and other vapors that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire.

  • Inspect the chimney and the chimney connector (the pipe between stove and chimney) at least once every two months during the heating season. If creosote has built up, have it removed.
  • At first, check for soot above the baffle plate and around the flue outlet every month or so.
  • If the stove suddenly turns sluggish, check for a soot fall around the flue collar or in the chimney.
  • Clean the whole flue, from the stove to the top of the chimney, after each heating season. Inspect it before the next season for bird's nests or other blockages.

Can't inspect or clean it yourself? Contact your Morsø dealer or a professional chimney sweep.

Chimney fire: close the air control, get everyone out of the house, and call the fire department.

Smoke coming into the room?

If smoke or fumes come out when you light or reload, or the fire won't respond, poor draft is almost certainly to blame. In a very few cases the room isn't getting enough fresh air. Ask your stove supplier how best to improve the flue system.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; contact can burn skin.
  • Keep furniture at least 30 inches away, and drying clothes, newspapers and firewood too. Don't keep wood within the clearances or the space you need for loading and ash removal.
  • Never start or freshen a fire with gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids.
  • Never leave the stove unattended with the door open.
  • Morsø recommends a smoke detector in the stove's room. Put at least one on each floor, close to sleeping areas and not too near the stove. Some areas require smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

Over-firing

Do not over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney connector glows, you are over-firing. That can cause a house fire or permanently damage the stove. A Morsø Flue Gas Thermometer (part # 62901200) on the stove pipe, about 20 cm (8") above the top plate, helps you judge the temperature:

Normalapprox. 300° C (550°F)
Never above450° C (750°F)
Note: p. 16 gives the flue-temperature limit as 450° C (750°F) and normal firing as approx. 300° C (550°F); in both pairs the Celsius and Fahrenheit figures don't match each other.

care.title: Yearly care & off-season
care.html:
Wear safety goggles and gloves for maintenance. Before each heating season, clean, inspect and repair:

  • Clean the chimney and chimney connector thoroughly; replace damaged sections.
  • Check the gaskets for wear or compression.
  • Check the glass for cracks, and the door and handle for tightness.

Door gasket

The door gasket can harden over time. Replace it if the door gets hard to close, or if air leaks in around it and the fire gets harder to control. Your stove supplier has a Morsø rope gasket kit.

Paint

Clean the painted surface with a soft-brush vacuum or a lint-free cloth. If it turns slightly gray, Morsø touch-up spray paint fixes it; ventilate the room the next time you fire the stove.

Leaving it unused

Clean it out thoroughly and leave the air control slightly open. Keep rain out with a chimney cap, but don't block the flue completely. Leftover ash soaks up moisture, which causes rust. A moisture absorber such as kitty litter in the ash pan helps over summer; take it out before the heating season.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
When the stove is supplied by an authorised Morsø dealer, Morsø gives a 10-year warranty against manufacturing defects in the main exterior body parts, from the date of purchase. Parts defective in materials or workmanship are repaired or replaced.

Not covered

  • Installation or use that doesn't follow the manual or local regulations
  • Damage from overheating or burning the wrong fuel
  • Normal wear, such as discolored surfaces, and wear parts: smoke deflector plates, grates, refractory stones and plates, glass and seals
  • The paint finish and ceramic rope (p. 18)
  • Repairs or changes Morsø hasn't authorized
  • Corrosion from lack of maintenance or a damaged surface finish
  • Problems from local conditions, draft or the chimney

The warranty is void if the stove isn't installed, run and maintained as the manual says, or if you burn materials it isn't EPA-certified for.

Making a claim

Contact Morsø Customer Service (info@morsoe.com or +45 96691900) with your proof of purchase, the model and serial number, and a description of the problem, with photos if you can.

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
Heat output11,892 to 19,067 Btu/hr (specific test conditions)
Efficiency74% (higher heating value), CSA B415.1
Particulate1.8 g/h, EPA Method 28 crib wood
EPA2020 particulate emission standards, crib wood
CO in flue0.8 gr/min average (p. 16)
ListingPFS TECO, report F20-581
StandardsANSI/UL-1482-2011 (R2015) US · ULC S627-00 Canada

Non-catalytic; listed for wood only. The minimum low burn rate is manufacturer-set and must not be altered (federal regulations). Data plate is on the back of the stove (p. 4).

specFlue.title: Chimney & flue
specFlue.html:
Flue sizenot less than 6" diameter (or equivalent cross section)
Chimney, USAlisted type HT factory-built, UL-103-1985 (2100° F), or code-approved masonry with flue liner
Chimney, CanadaHigh Temperature (650°C) ULC S-629
Heightat least 16 feet above the stove recommended (not required), flue collar to chimney top

One flueway per appliance: never connect to a flue serving another appliance. The flue system must be independently secured, not supported by the stove. Don't oversize it: too large a section cools the flue gases and makes the stove sluggish or unpredictable. Roof construction, nearby trees and high altitude can affect draft and height; consult a local chimney sweep or Morsø dealer.

Flue temperature (p. 16)

In the stove pipe, 20 cm above the stove: approx. 300° C (550°F) under normal firing; must not exceed 450° C (750°F), which counts as over-firing.

Note: p. 16 pairs the flue-temperature limit of 450° C with 750°F (and normal firing at 300° C with 550°F); the Celsius and Fahrenheit figures are not equivalent.

specConnector.title: Chimney connector
specConnector.html:
Diameter6 inches (150mm)
Single wall24 gauge or heavier steel (24 MSG black or blue); never galvanized
Double walltested and listed for solid fuel
Horizontal runrecommended max 3 feet (1 metre)
Total lengthno longer than 8 feet (2.5 metres)
Slopeup 1/4 inch per foot (20 mm per metre) toward the chimney
Turnsno more than two 90 degree
Horizontal run to ceiling18 inches
Fastenersmin. three screws at the stove and each joint

A connector is required; don't install the chimney directly at the stove outlet. Use mild bends (45° rather than 90°) in one continuous section, keep it all accessible for cleaning, and seal every joint airtight to the chimney outlet. Never through an attic, closet or similar concealed space; avoid combustible walls and ceilings, and make any combustible wall pass-through to CAN/CSA-B365.

Rear outlet

Knock out the round panel in the rear heat shield plate to reveal the cast iron plate. Untwist the blanking plate and the flue collar, swap their positions, push down and tighten the enclosed screws.

Wear gloves and eye protection when drilling, cutting or joining connector.

specClear.html:

Increase distances for heat-sensitive materials; wallpaper and decorations can detach with heat. Furniture: 30 inches recommended minimum (p. 9).

Note: the general text on p. 8 says never to install the stove within 8 inches of combustibles at the sides or 16 inches above the top; the clearance tables on pp. 8–9 give 10" sidewall to unit (12" in an alcove) and 54.5" unit to ceiling (24.5" in an alcove).

specAlcove.title: Alcove installation
specAlcove.html:
Double-wall connector only. Inches apply in the USA, mm (in parentheses) in Canada.

A · Sidewall to unit12" (305 mm)
B · Backwall to unit3" (76 mm)
D · Sidewall to connector17" (432 mm)
E · Backwall to connector7.5" (190 mm)
G · Unit to ceiling24.5" (622 mm)
H · Floor to ceiling54" (1372 mm)
Max alcove depth32" (813mm)

No cornerwall values are given for an alcove. The floor protector must be non-combustible and extend beneath the heater and to the front, sides and rear; the manual shows the alcove floor-protection layout as a diagram on this page.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
The heater meets CAN/ULC-S627: it suits a combustible floor and needs no radiant floor protection (p. 8), but it does need ember protection. Table values: inches for the USA, mm for Canada.

Front16" · 450 mm
Right side6" · 200 mm
Left side6" · 200 mm
Back– · 200 mm
Rear exitbeneath the connector and 2 inches beyond each side (p. 8)

US: non-combustible material, beneath the heater and 16" to the front and 6" to the sides of the fuel loading door and ash removal openings.

Canada (CSA B365): continuous, durable non-combustible ember pad at least 450 mm (18 in) beyond any side with a door, for the full width plus 200 mm (8 in) each side, and 200 mm (8 in) beyond other sides. Less than 200 mm (8 in) from a wall, it need only reach the base of the wall. Not on carpet unless structurally supported.

specFuel.title: Fuel & loading
specFuel.html:
Fuelwood only
Log lengthmax 12 inches (30 cm)
Maker's website: Log Size 11".
Log sectionapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)
Moistureno more than 20%
Kindling, first light2-4 pounds
Refuel load3 lbs (2 pieces) up to 6 lbs (5 pieces)
Max per load6 lbs (5 split logs)

Keep the load below the stainless-steel secondary air supply box on the firebox back wall; the space in front and above is for volatile gas combustion only. Build the fire directly on the hearth: no grate, andirons or other elevation.

Note: p. 12 gives the log thickness as approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm); p. 28 says the wood must be split and 8 - 12 cm thick.
Note: pp. 15–16 give the load size as up to 6 lbs (5 pieces); p. 28 says to refuel with 2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg.

specMobile.title: Mobile home & combustion air
specMobile.html:
USA only. In Canada, do not install in a transportable building or mobile home.

Combustion airoutside combustion air kit
Connector & chimneylisted Type HT connector and HT chimney
Terminal capwith spark arrestor
Anchoringbolted through the hearth pad into the flooring
Code24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD)
Transporttop chimney sections removable for max. 13.5' from ground level
Outside-air bracketSKU 71613700 (p. 25)
  • Never a single-wall connector (stovepipe).
  • Follow the section 1.5 floor protection precisely.
  • Install the outside air kit per its own guide; intake piping through the floor into a vented crawl space, or through the wall.
  • Never draw combustion air from a wall, floor or ceiling cavity or an enclosed space such as an attic or garage.
  • Not in a sleeping room. Keep the structure intact: don't cut joists, studs or trusses.

Fresh-air inlet

Unless the room gets enough ambient air leakage through doors and windows, a dedicated inlet with 2 square inches (1250 square mm) of free air space is needed, especially in a well-sealed room or with an extractor hood or ventilation system. Not on a wall usually under negative wind pressure, and not directly across the room from the stove.

review.notes: The manual covers the whole Morsø 6100 B series (cover: Morsø 6100 B); the 6148 B is named only on the parts diagram (p. 23), and the clearance and floor-protection tables are not broken out by model. The catalog's model number does not appear in the manual. The manual gives no dimensions, weight, firebox volume, heating area or outside-air kit part number (only the bracket, SKU 71613700), so those catalog specs could not be checked; output, efficiency, emissions, EPA status, flue size, top/rear outlet, non-catalytic and US mobile-home approval all match the catalog. p. 7 has no text (figure only) and was not used. The p. 9 alcove floor-protection drawing and the p. 23 parts diagram are referenced, not transcribed. The manual says not to use a grate to elevate the fire (pp. 11-12) but its ash steps refer to ash slots in the grate (p. 19); both kept as written. p. 8 mentions fireplace installations although p. 4 says do not install in any fireplace; fireplace installs are not described. The mobile-home list (p. 11) includes a Canadian chimney requirement although it says not to install in Canadian mobile homes; the guide treats mobile homes as US only. 'kitter litter' (p. 22) rendered as kitty litter. No troubleshooting chart or code table: fault panels are built from the manual's draft, over-firing, dirty-glass and gasket descriptions (pp. 5, 13, 16-18).
